population: End of the monarchy. The archaic city of about 285 ha (Ampolo, Cornell) may have held 20,000-40,000; Plutarch's census of 130,000 for 508 BC (Publicola 12) counts the whole citizen body of the territory and is doubtful.
Gallic sack; afterwards the 11 km Servian Wall (from 378 BC) encloses 426 ha, far more than was built up.
Aqua Appia, the first aqueduct, and the Via Appia: the city outgrows its springs.
Start of the First Punic War; Rome the largest city of Italy after Tarentum and Capua.
After the Second Punic War, refugees and freed slaves swell the plebs.
Age of the Gracchi: land crisis drives migration to the city; Gaius Gracchus' grain law of 123.
Lex Terentia Cassia (73) restores grain sales; perhaps 40,000 recipients rising fast.
Clodius makes the grain ration free (58); recipients soar to 320,000 adult male citizens by 46.
Caesar's revision of the lists cuts recipients from 320,000 to 150,000 (Suetonius Iul. 41.3), partly by settling 80,000 colonists overseas.

Augustus pays 60 denarii each to 320,000 of the urban plebs in 5 BC (Res Gestae 15) and limits grain recipients to about 200,000 in 2 BC (Dio 55.10.1). Adding women, children, slaves, soldiers and foreigners gives the 'Great Rome' figure of about 1 million (Lo Cascio, Morley, Hopkins); Storey's density method gives about 450,000.
Death of Augustus. Strabo describes continuous building and the 70-foot height limit.
Great Fire: of 14 regions, 3 destroyed and 7 badly damaged (Tacitus Ann. 15.40).
Trajanic peak of public building; Trajan lowers the height limit to 60 feet.
Antonine plague arrives with the army returning from the East; mortality in the city perhaps 10-20 per cent over the following decades.
Severan Rome; the plebs frumentaria perhaps 150,000-200,000 men; the Marble Plan maps the city.
The Aurelian Wall (19 km) encloses 1,372 ha; Aurelian replaces grain with free bread and adds pork, oil and cheap wine.
Constantine. The Regionary Catalogues of the mid-4th century count 46,602 insulae and 1,790 domus, 290 horrea, 254 bakeries.
Constantius II's visit (Ammianus 16.10) finds a city of overwhelming monuments.
Krautheimer's figure of about 800,000 is a high estimate; many now prefer 500,000 or less for the late 4th century.
Alaric's first siege brings famine and plague (Zosimus 5.39).
Pork distribution data (Nov. Val. 36) have been used to estimate 120,000-200,000 recipients and a population of perhaps 400,000-500,000 in the early 5th century.
Valentinian III lowers the pork contributions owing to fewer consumers; the fall since 410 is clear but its size disputed.
Vandal sack (14 days of plunder); captives carried to Carthage.
Theodoric's visit; restorations by the Ostrogothic kings. Cassiodorus still speaks of a large populace living on the old supply system.
Gothic siege of 537-538: aqueducts cut, the hills lose their water and their people.
Totila takes the city; Procopius (Wars 7.22.19) claims it was left with no inhabitants at all for 40 days, a rhetorical exaggeration.
End of the Gothic War: the population, concentrated in the Campus Martius and Trastevere, is put at about 30,000 by Krautheimer.
Plague and flood; Gregory organises food relief through the church's estates and diaconiae.
Early medieval city of perhaps 30,000-60,000 inside a wall built for ten times as many.

populationDebate.position: Imperial Rome about 750,000-1,000,000; Augustan census figures count adult males, so the citizen population was large.
About 1 million under Augustus, built from the grain-dole recipients plus women, children, slaves and foreigners.

populationDebate.scholar: Hermansen, 'The population of imperial Rome: the Regionaries', Historia 27 (1978)
populationDebate.position: Examined the 46,602 'insulae' of the Regionary Catalogues and argued they must be units of property or apartments rather than whole blocks, which removes them as evidence against a large population.

populationDebate.scholar: Lo Cascio, 'The size of the Roman population', JRS 84 (1994) and later studies
populationDebate.position: Defends a population of roughly 1 million (or more) under Augustus, while arguing for a low Italian total; reads the frumentationes and the recensus as evidence of a very large plebs.
About 1 million, with the city's demand transforming the economy of Italy; Rome kept up its numbers by constant immigration because urban mortality exceeded births.

populationDebate.scholar: Storey, 'The population of ancient Rome', Antiquity 71 (1997)
populationDebate.position: Applying densities from Pompeii and Ostia to the 13.86 sq km inside the Aurelian Wall gives about 440,000 (Ostia density) or 335,000 (average): 'of the order of half a million'.

populationDebate.scholar: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980)
populationDebate.position: Late-antique decline from perhaps 800,000 around 400 to some 30,000 after the Gothic War, with the people withdrawing from the hills (disabitato) into the river bend (abitato).

populationDebate.scholar: Durliat, De la ville antique à la ville byzantine (1990); Barnish, PBSR 55 (1987)
populationDebate.position: Use the 5th-century pork and grain figures to reconstruct the fall; Barnish warns that the 452 law is too rhetorical to give firm numbers.

densityScale: density 0-1 is the intensity of residential occupation (1 = continuous tenement fabric as in the Subura under the early empire). Types: huts, houses (atrium houses and small dwellings), domus (large aristocratic houses), insulae (multi-storey tenements), mixed (houses, shops and workshops), villas (suburban farms and villas), horti (landscaped gardens), cemetery, public (monumental or state land with few residents), abandoned (ruins, fields and vineyards inside the walls: the disabitato). Each phase lasts until the next phase's 'from'.

rules.rule: Lex Icilia de Aventino publicando: public land on the Aventine distributed to plebeians for houses; several families could share one building by storeys.
First recorded multi-storey building: an ox climbed to the third storey of a house in the Forum Boarium (prodigy of 218 BC), showing tenements of three floors by then.
Vitruvius: Rome's population and limited space forced building upward; party walls could be only 1.5 feet thick, so tall blocks used concrete and brick piers.
Augustus divides the city into 14 regions and 265 vici with elected vicomagistri; he creates the vigiles (AD 6) and sets a maximum height of 70 feet (20.7 m) for buildings on public streets.

After the Great Fire Nero's building code: wider straight streets, limited heights, open courtyards, porticoes on the street fronts paid by the emperor, fire-proof Gabine or Alban stone in lower walls, no shared party walls, water tanks for fire-fighting.
Senatus consultum Hosidianum forbids demolishing buildings to sell their materials for profit (renewed by the SC Acilianum of 122).
Trajan lowers the maximum height of private buildings to 60 feet (17.8 m).
Juvenal on insulae: buildings propped up by beams, constant collapses and fires; the poor live under the tiles where the pigeons nest.
Regionary Catalogues record 46,602 insulae and 1,790 domus in the 14 regions (Notitia), with 254 bakeries, 290 warehouses, 856 baths, 1,352 fountains, 144 latrines and 28 libraries.
Majorian forbids demolishing public buildings for materials, a sign that the shrinking city was already quarrying itself.
The Goths cut all the aqueducts; except for the Aqua Traiana (patched later) and wells, the hills lose their water supply and are abandoned for the river bend.

fires.name: Fire between the Salinae and the Porta Carmentalis
fires.burnt: Burned for two nights and a day everything between the Salinae (salt stores by the Porta Trigemina) and the Porta Carmentalis, including the Aequimaelium and Vicus Iugarius and the temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta, and beyond the gate many sacred and profane buildings.
fires.rebuilding: Temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta rebuilt in 212 BC.

fires.name: Arson in the Forum
fires.burnt: Fire started at night at several points round the Forum: the seven shops (later five), the bankers' shops (later Tabernae Novae), private houses, the Lautumiae, the Forum Piscarium and the Atrium Regium burned; the Temple of Vesta was barely saved. Campanian nobles were convicted of arson.
fires.rebuilding: Tabernae and markets rebuilt by the censors of 209 and 179 BC; Basilica Fulvia (Aemilia) in 179.

fires.name: Fire in the Forum Boarium
fires.burnt: A fire in the Forum Boarium burned for a day and a night; all the buildings facing the Tiber and the shops with valuable goods were destroyed.
fires.rebuilding: Rebuilt; the Emporium below the Aventine (193 BC) took over the main harbour function.

fires.name: Fire on the Palatine (Temple of Magna Mater)
fires.burnt: The Temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine burned; the extent of the fire beyond it is unknown.
fires.rebuilding: Temple rebuilt by a Metellus (probably Q. Caecilius Metellus Numidicus).
fires.note: Date 111 BC from Obsequens' prodigy list is likely but not certain.

fires.name: Burning of the Curia at Clodius' funeral
fires.burnt: Clodius' supporters carried his body into the Curia Hostilia and burned it on a pyre of benches and records; the Senate house and the adjoining Basilica Porcia were destroyed.
fires.rebuilding: Faustus Sulla rebuilt the Curia; Caesar replaced it with the Curia Iulia.

fires.name: Arson by freedmen: Circus Maximus and Temple of Ceres
fires.burnt: Freedmen protesting a war tax set fires that burned much of the Circus Maximus, the Temple of Ceres and the Temple of Spes.

fires.name: Fire of the Basilica Aemilia
fires.burnt: The Basilica Paulli (Aemilia) burned, the fire spreading to the Temple of Vesta, whose sacred objects the Vestals carried to the Palatine.
fires.rebuilding: Rebuilt by Aemilius Paullus with Augustus' help.

fires.name: Fires of AD 6
fires.burnt: Many parts of the city burned in AD 6 (Dio does not name them); the disaster led Augustus to create the seven cohorts of vigiles.
fires.rebuilding: Vigiles created, financed by a 2 per cent tax on slave sales.
fires.note: No location given in the sources; no polygon.

fires.name: Fire on the Caelian
fires.burnt: The whole Caelian hill burned; a statue of Tiberius in the house of the senator Iunius was the only thing that survived, and the Senate proposed renaming the hill Mons Augustus.
fires.rebuilding: Tiberius paid for losses according to each owner's damage.

fires.name: Fire on the Aventine and around the Circus
fires.burnt: Fire burned the part of the Circus Maximus next to the Aventine and the buildings on the Aventine itself.
fires.rebuilding: Tiberius paid 100 million sesterces in compensation.

fires.name: Great Fire of Rome
fires.burnt: Broke out on 18-19 July in shops at the Palatine-Caelian end of the Circus Maximus, burned for six days, then broke out again from the Aemilian estates (second polygon, southern Campus Martius by the Capitol) for three more. Of the 14 regions, 3 were levelled (usually identified as III, X, XI), 7 left with a few gutted buildings, and 4 untouched (I, V, VI, XIV). Temples of Luna, Jupiter Stator, Vesta and the Regia burned.
fires.rebuilding: Nero's building code; the Domus Aurea occupied some 80 ha of the burned centre until the Flavians returned it to public use.
fires.note: Region identifications follow the common reading of Tacitus; the polygon covers regions III, X, XI fully and the adjoining parts of II, IV, VIII, XII and XIII.

fires.name: Burning of the Capitol
fires.burnt: On 19 December 69, during the fighting between Vitellius' troops and the Flavian party besieged on the Capitol, the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the buildings round the Capitol burned.
fires.rebuilding: Vespasian rebuilt the temple (dedicated 75), clearing the rubble himself.

fires.name: Fire of AD 80 in the Campus Martius
fires.burnt: A three-day fire burned the Temple of Serapis and Isis, the Saepta, the Temple of Neptune, the Baths of Agrippa, the Pantheon, the Diribitorium, the Theatre of Balbus, the stage of Pompey's theatre, the Porticus Octaviae with its libraries, and the Capitoline temple.
fires.rebuilding: Titus and Domitian rebuilt; Domitian's programme renewed most of the Campus Martius.

fires.name: Fire of 192
fires.burnt: Starting at night, perhaps from an earthquake or lightning, the fire destroyed the Templum Pacis with its libraries and the Horrea Piperataria (where Galen lost his books and drugs), reached the Temple of Vesta and the palace on the Palatine.
fires.rebuilding: Restored by Septimius Severus; the Marble Plan was set up in the rebuilt Templum Pacis.

fires.name: Fire under Carinus
fires.burnt: Burned the Senate house, the Forum of Caesar, the Basilica Iulia and the Graecostadium.
fires.rebuilding: Diocletian and Maximian rebuilt the Curia and the Basilica Iulia.

fires.name: Fires of Alaric's sack
fires.burnt: The Goths burned the houses by the Salarian gate including the palace in the Horti Sallustiani, the Basilica Aemilia (coins fused into its floor) and the Secretarium Senatus, and plundered and burned houses on the Aventine.
fires.rebuilding: Partial restorations: the Secretarium Senatus by the urban prefect Epiphanius (412), the Basilica Aemilia rebuilt in reduced form.

floodExtents.note: Low ground of the Campus Martius, the Velabrum and Forum Boarium and the river bank of Trastevere, flooded in ordinary high floods (river about 13-14 m above sea level at the Ripetta).
Great floods (river 17-19 m) reached the Forum, the Circus valley, almost the whole Campus Martius including the Pantheon and the Via Lata, and the Trastevere lowland.

floods.t: Flood followed by fire destroyed all the buildings in the low-lying city.
Tiber flooded the low parts of the city twice.
The Ludi Apollinares were moved because the Circus Maximus was under water.
Flood around the Porta Flumentana; buildings collapsed.
Two floods destroyed the bridges and buildings near the Porta Flumentana.
Twelve floods in one year covered the Campus Martius and low parts of the city.
Great flood blamed on Gabinius' acquittal; Cicero describes the devastation.
Flood on the night Octavian was named Augustus, taken as an omen.
Flood carried away the Pons Sublicius and made the city navigable for three days.
Flood with plague and famine; the people offer Augustus the dictatorship.
Flood on Augustus' return; Balbus reached his new theatre by boat.
Flood made the city navigable for seven days.
Flood destroyed buildings and drowned people; Tiberius appoints five curators of the river banks and channel.
Sudden flood broke the Pons Sublicius, filled the low city and caused famine as Otho set out.
Severe flood destroyed buildings and caused famine at the start of Marcus Aurelius' reign.
The Tiber overflowed the walls and destroyed many old buildings and church granaries; plague followed, killing Pope Pelagius II.

note: Zones are drawn to the hills and valleys; boundaries are generalised. Phase values are judgements from the literary sources, the Regionary Catalogues and excavation, following Coarelli, Carandini's Atlas, Krautheimer and Lo Cascio/Storey for overall totals. The late-antique pattern follows Krautheimer: after 410 and especially after 537 the people drew back to the Campus Martius bend, Trastevere, the Via Lata and the riverside below the Capitol, with smaller clusters at the Lateran, Santa Maria Maggiore and St Peter's.
